[guideline: SKIN DISEASES p96] HEAD LICE contagious. - Diagnosis of active lice infestation is made by observing a live, moving louse on the scalp. MANAGEMENT Family and close physical contacts should be examined and treated if live lice are found. Wash bedding, combs and brushes thoroughly in hot water. WET COMBING - Use a fine-toothed comb after applying a generous amount of hair conditioner to wet hair. - Repeat the process everyday for 10 to 14 days until no lice are found. - This method works in about half of patients - Alternatively, topical insecticides can be used: - Permethrin 1% topically, leave for a minimum for 20 minute before washing out All lice treatments should be repeated 7 days later. Wash hands thoroughly after using lice treatments. Treatment failure may be due to incorrectly applied treatment or re-infestation.

Check for live moving lice on the scalp to make the diagnosis certain.
He feeds well and has no danger signs, so treat here: wet comb daily with conditioner for 10 to 14 days, or apply permethrin 1% for 20 minutes then wash.
Repeat treatment after 7 days, and wash all bedding and combs in hot water.
Check mother and any siblings for lice too.
Send him in the truck only if sores become very red and swollen, he gets a fever, or stops feeding well.

[guideline: PAEDIATRIC PHARMACY ADVICE p14] GIVING MEDICINES TO CHILDREN Rectal medicines - Use of gloves is recommended when inserting a suppository - Position the child on their left side with the upper leg bent and buttocks separated - Moisten the suppository with lubricating jelly to help with insertion - Insert gently to about half the length of the finger o For a bullet shaped suppository, insert the pointy end first o For a tear-drop shaped suppository, insert the larger rounded end first - Hold the buttocks together for five minutes to stop the suppository being expelled - Have the child lie down or sit for about 10 minutes - Discourage the child from going to the toilet after the suppository has been given Eye medicines - Wash your hands - Clean the eyes with a clean, damp towel - Tilt head back - small children can lay on their back - Make sure the dropper does not touch the eyes or eyelashes - Pull down gently on lower eye lid - Drop the solution or squeeze 1.5cm of ointment into eyelid - Have the child close the eye for one minute - Apply pressure to the inner corner of the eye to stop the loss of medication through the duct - If giving more than one drop then wait five minutes in between drops to make sure everything gets absorbed Note: eye ointments can temporarily blur vision Ear medicines - Put child on their side - Straighten the ear canal o For infants the ear should be pulled back and down o For older children the ear should be pulled back and up. - The child should remain on their side for five minutes to allow the drops to enter the ear - Cotton wool can be used as a plug to prevent the drops from running out of the ear

Boy 144 months, 40.3 kg, has hot body and complains of ear pain. He is drinking and no vomiting, no fit. We have RDT and ACT, and transport is available now. Please tell me the steps.
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: THE 10-STEP CHECKLIST FOR CHILDREN
---
Step 1: he is drinking and awake with no convulsions, so no general danger sign.
Step 2: ask about cough and difficult breathing, count breaths and look for chest in-drawing and stridor.
Step 3: ask about diarrhoea and check for dehydration.
Step 4: do a malaria RDT and look for signs of malaria, meningitis and other infections.
Step 5: check the ears for middle ear infection and mastoiditis, and treat as per the ear section if positive.
Step 6 to 9: look for pallor, check both feet for oedema, weigh him, give due vaccines and feeding advice. Return in 2 days or sooner if danger signs appear.

assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NOW
STM: MALARIA
---
Convulsion with a positive RDT is severe malaria. Refer now.
Call the AHC or hospital on the radio or phone and arrange transport today; do not wait.
If you have artesunate, give 2.4 mg/kg (about 30 mg) IM before transfer; if not, give artesunate PR 10 mg/kg (about 124 mg).
Check blood sugar and lay the child on the side; watch for more fits.
Send the weight, RDT result and time of the fit with the child.

8 month bebi, 7.3 kg, watery stool since yesterday, eye sink small, restless, want dring. Skin pinch go bak slow. No RDT stock. Next bot go long Tuesday. No blad, no fever.
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: DIARRHOEA
---
Some dehydration (restless, sunken eyes, thirsty, slow skin pinch), so start ORS now at the clinic.
ORS: 20 ml per kg over 4 hours = about 145 ml for 7.3 kg, give very slowly with teaspoon to prevent vomiting.
Zinc sulphate 10 mg orally once daily for 14 days (bebi is under 6 months? No, 8 months, so give 20 mg once daily).
Antibiotics not needed because no blood in stool.
If eyelids get puffy, stop ORS and review after 3 hours.
Danger signs: floppy, drinks poorly, very slow skin pinch, blood in stool, vomits everything. If any appear before Tuesday boat, call AHC by radio urgently; if transport is absolutely needed earlier, send with family by any available means.

[guideline: PERTUSSIS (WHOOPING COUGH) p81] Whooping cough occurs when the bacteria Bordetella pertussis gets into the respiratory tract and causes a bloody mucous to be formed CAUSE - Spread by air droplets - Patients are contagious for 21 days after the onset of the cough, if untreated - Non-vaccinated children most commonly affected. Can occur in immunised children but usually a more mild illness SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Cough and runny nose for 1 week (1st stage) followed by spasmodic cough with 'whooping' sound. May also present as a non-specific persistant cough - Vomiting often following a coughing spasm - Apnoea or cyanosis during coughing spasms - Fever is uncommon - There may be no clinical signs on examination and children may appear well between coughing spasms COMPLICATIONS - Infants < 6 months are at greatest risk and are commonly infected by family members - Apnoea - Severe pneumonia - Encephalopathy INVESTIGATIONS - Generally a clinical diagnosis - If persistant cough or other suggestive symptoms (weight loss, night sweats) remember to assess TB exposure and consider investigations if risk factors - Blood count (may be associated with high lymphocyte count) MANAGEMENT MANAGEMENT NOTES:

[guideline: ASTHMA p21] - Asthma is caused by reversible tightening (bronchospasm) and inflammation in the airways - Children with asthma usually have recurrent episodes of wheeze and cough that improves with salbutamol - Think about asthma in any child older than 1 year who has shortness of breath, cough and wheeze. SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - The most important signs of severity are general appearance/mental state and increased work of breathing. Wheeze is a poor predictor of severity. - Rapid breathing ("short wind"), tachycardia, difficulty talking - Chest tightness, prolonged expiratory phase - Improvement in symptoms with salbutamol - Cough may be only at night or during activity - Low oxygen saturations may be a late sign - A silent chest is a pre-terminal sign
Baby only 2 months, 4.5 kg. He wheezing since this morning, now his chest very quiet when I listen, no air entry I can hear. No transport today, boat broke down and no truck coming.
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NOW
STM: ASTHMA
---
Silent chest in a young baby is very dangerous, this is severe asthma.
Call the AHC or hospital by radio or phone right now, ask for emergency advice and possible boat dispatch.
Give salbutamol 0.5 mL of 5 mg/mL solution in 2 mL normal saline by nebuliser with oxygen driving it if you have, or 2 puffs via spacer with mask.
Keep baby warm, head slightly elevated, watch his colour and breathing, be ready for resuscitation.
Repeat salbutamol every 20 minutes until help comes or transport arrives.
Write referral note: age 2 months, weight 4.5 kg, silent chest, no air entry, salbutamol given with times, no transport available, radio call made.

[guideline: MALARIA p53] INVESTIGATION - Malaria slide (MPS) OR Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) - Blood glucose MANAGEMENT - Consider malaria in any child with a fever. Check MPS or RDT - Note the type of malaria (thin film) and the parasite count (thick film) - A single negative film or antigen does not exclude malaria - If strong suspicion, thick and thin films should be repeated with fever spikes until positive test or 3 negatives obtained - RDT can remain positive for up to 6 weeks after malaria has been treated - Always think about other infections, even if the MPS or RDT is positive - A child with fever and decreased conciousness might have meningitis - Classify as uncomplicated versus complicated and manage accordingly If you cannot test for malaria, treat presumptively Very sick children should be treated for severe malaria
Bebi 9 manis, 7.3 kilo. RDT positive. Hemi hot bodi, skin pale-pale, slip tumas. Bot blong go Auki bae go tumoro moning. No garem ACT long klinik.
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: MALARIA
---
Pallor an slip tumas hem saen blong denja. Complicated malaria. Pikinini mas go long hospital long bot tumoro.
Taem yu wet: givim artesunate 17.5 mg IM (2.4 mg fo evri kilo) nao, an givim moa long 12 aoa.
Sapos no artesunate IM, givim artesunate 73 mg long anus (10 mg fo evri kilo).
Lukim blood sugar sapos yu save. Givim susu o sweet dring sapos hem fit.
Kipim bebi warm, letem mama oflankem hem. No letem wet fo bot long san.
Raetem referral: 9 manis, 7.3 kg, RDT positive, pallor, slip tumas, artesunate taem an dose.

[guideline: FEVER p40] - Fever is defined as an axillary (under the arm) temperature greater than 37.5 oC - Fever in itself is not dangerous as it helps the body to fight infection CAUSES The common causes of fever in children are: - Common viral infections: upper respiratory tract infection, measles, gastroenteritis - Common bacterial: pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, urinary tract infections - Other: Malaria, tuberculosis INVESTIGATIONS - Consider blood film or rapid diagnostic test for malaria parasites - If possible, collect and test a urine sample MANAGEMENT - Treat the cause of the fever - Consider antimalarials - Consider giving paracetamol if fever above 38ºC AND the child is irritable o Dose: 15mg/kg (max 1g) every 4 to 6 hours (maximum 4 doses in 24 hours) o Do not use aspirin in children for fever - Give extra fluids Consider the following causes for fever greater than 7 days: - Abscess - Salmonella infection - Infective endocarditis - Rheumatic fever - Tuberculosis Fever helps the body to fight infection Try to find and treat the cause of the fever

assistant:

---
Do a malaria RDT now and treat the result as the manual says.
If fever is above 38 and the child is irritable, give paracetamol 102 mg (15 mg/kg) by mouth every 4 to 6 hours, maximum 4 doses in 24 hours.

Come back in 2 days, or at once if the child cannot drink, vomits everything, fits, or becomes floppy.

This newborn at our village clinic was born 5 days ago at home, weight 2.4 kg. The mother says baby not feeding well since yesterday, feels hot, umbilical cord stump is red and smelly. No transport available here, we only have radio. What should we do?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NOW
STM: NEWBORN BABIES - NEONATAL INFECTIONS
---
This is neonatal infection with danger signs: poor feeding, fever, and umbilical redness with pus. Age under 2 months with fever is a red flag.
Call the hospital or AHC by radio now to arrange urgent pickup or boat. Start cefotaxime 120 mg IV or IM (50 mg per kilo) every 8 hours if you can give it.
Keep baby warm, skin to skin with mother. Try to express breast milk and give by cup or spoon if baby too weak to suck.
Write referral note: age 5 days, weight 2.4 kg, fever, poor feeding, umbilical erythema and discharge, antibiotics given with times.
Tell mother to keep trying feeds and watch for breathing problems or fits on the way.

[guideline: MALARIA p53] OTHER SUPPORTIVE MEASURES - If child is fitting, check BSL and treat with anti-convulsants - Fitting may be secondary to cerebral malaria, febrile convulsions or meningitis - Treat with antibiotics for meningitis - Perform a lumbar puncture once stable - Hypoglycaemia is a feature of malaria (and a side effect of quinine treatment) - Check blood sugar every 6 hours if severe malaria or on quinine - For hypoglycaemia management refer to hypoglycaemia guideline - Caution with fluid/balance as patients with malaria are vulnerable to fluid overload and pulmonary oedema - Monitor and treat for other complications including: - Severe anaemia: give packed red cell transfusion - Metabolic acidosis: give oxygen, IV fluids - Acute renal failure - Spontaneous bleeding/coagulopathy - Consider discharge when afebrile for 24 hours and able to tolerate oral medications MALARIA PREVENTION - Encourage all families to sleep under a mosqito net. - Mosquito nets should be impregnated with a chemical insecticide. - They can be obtained from the Ministry of Health
Pikinini 54 month, 18.1 kilo. Hem garem hot bodi an skin blong hem pale tumas. Hem sek-sek long moning ya. Nao hem no fit dring, hem toroaot evri samting. Mi no garem RDT an no garem artemether tablet. Wanem nao mi mas duim?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NOW
STM: MALARIA
---
Sek-sek an no fit dring an toroaot evri samting hem olketa saen blong denja. Skin pale tu. Diswan hem severe malaria o meningtis. Sendem go long hospital kwiktaem.
Taem yu wet: givim artesunate 43 mg (2.4 mg fo evri kilo) IM nao. Sapos yu no garem artesunate IM, givim 181 mg long anus (10 mg fo evri kilo).
Lukim blood sugar, hypoglycaemia hem feature blong malaria.
Putum pikinini long saed, no putum eni samting long maot sapos hem sek-sek moa.
Kolem dokta long AHC o hospital long radio o fon nao.
No givim tumas fluid, malaria pikinini save kasem fluid overload.

SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Fever, cough,fast breathing, increased work of breathing - Poor feeding, vomiting, chest or abdominal pain SEVERITY OF PNEUMONIA MILD MODERATE SEVERE Respiratory rate Normal or increased Increased Markedly increased Accessory muscle use Mild or absent Mild-moderate Markedly increased - intercostal recession - subcostal recession - nasal flare - grunting, head bob Oral intake Normal or reduced Often reduced Reduced/no intake Cyanosis Not present Unlikely May be present Conscious state Alert, active Usually alert Drowsy/lethargic May be distressed/agitated
Sik pikinini ia hem 54 months, weight around 17.8 kg. Hem cough for three days and breathing fast, maybe 48 breaths in one minute, but no chest indrawing and he still drinks and eats fine. Boat to the clinic goes tomorrow morning, so what can I do tonight?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT
STM: PNEUMONIA
---
This looks like moderate pneumonia, so send him on the next boat to the clinic tomorrow morning.
While you wait, give amoxycillin 712 mg (40 mg/kg) by mouth every 12 hours, starting tonight.
Give paracetamol 267 mg (15 mg/kg) if he has fever, and keep him drinking water and breast milk.
Check his breathing every few hours; if he starts grunting, chest indrawing or cannot drink, call the AHC by radio and go sooner.
Write in the referral note: age, weight, breathing rate, cough, and the amoxycillin doses and times you gave.

Five day old baby 3.6 kg delivered at home with traditional birth attendant. Not passed urine today, very sleepy, mother says baby feels cold then hot, umbilical cord black but base is very red with pus. No transport here, no phone signal, only HF radio to AHC. What now?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NOW
STM: NEWBORN BABIES - NEONATAL INFECTIONS
---
Severe neonatal infection: poor feeding, altered temperature, lethargy and purulent umbilicus in a 5 day old baby. This needs immediate hospital care.
Give cefotaxime 180 mg IM or IV now if you can (50 mg per kilo), then every 8 hours. Call the AHC on HF radio for emergency evacuation plan or flying doctor.
Keep baby warm, skin to skin with mother under blanket. Try to wake for feeds, express milk and give by dropper or spoon if too sleepy.
Write referral note: age 5 days, weight 3.6 kg, poor feeding, temperature instability, lethargy, no urine today, umbilical infection with purulent discharge, antibiotics given.
Monitor closely until help comes: breathing rate, colour, fits. Tell mother to keep baby close and alert you if anything changes.

[guideline: ASTHMA p21] ASTHMA MANAGEMENT PLAN When sending a child with asthma home, it is useful to write down a plan for the parents to follow. [guideline: PERTUSSIS (WHOOPING COUGH) p81] Whooping cough occurs when the bacteria Bordetella pertussis gets into the respiratory tract and causes a bloody mucous to be formed CAUSE - Spread by air droplets - Patients are contagious for 21 days after the onset of the cough, if untreated - Non-vaccinated children most commonly affected. Can occur in immunised children but usually a more mild illness SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Cough and runny nose for 1 week (1st stage) followed by spasmodic cough with 'whooping' sound. May also present as a non-specific persistant cough - Vomiting often following a coughing spasm - Apnoea or cyanosis during coughing spasms - Fever is uncommon - There may be no clinical signs on examination and children may appear well between coughing spasms COMPLICATIONS - Infants < 6 months are at greatest risk and are commonly infected by family members - Apnoea - Severe pneumonia - Encephalopathy INVESTIGATIONS - Generally a clinical diagnosis - If persistant cough or other suggestive symptoms (weight loss, night sweats) remember to assess TB exposure and consider investigations if risk factors - Blood count (may be associated with high lymphocyte count) MANAGEMENT MANAGEMENT NOTES:

[guideline: FEVER p40] - Fever is defined as an axillary (under the arm) temperature greater than 37.5 oC - Fever in itself is not dangerous as it helps the body to fight infection CAUSES The common causes of fever in children are: - Common viral infections: upper respiratory tract infection, measles, gastroenteritis - Common bacterial: pneumonia, meningitis, otitis media, urinary tract infections - Other: Malaria, tuberculosis INVESTIGATIONS - Consider blood film or rapid diagnostic test for malaria parasites - If possible, collect and test a urine sample MANAGEMENT - Treat the cause of the fever - Consider antimalarials - Consider giving paracetamol if fever above 38ºC AND the child is irritable o Dose: 15mg/kg (max 1g) every 4 to 6 hours (maximum 4 doses in 24 hours) o Do not use aspirin in children for fever - Give extra fluids Consider the following causes for fever greater than 7 days: - Abscess - Salmonella infection - Infective endocarditis - Rheumatic fever - Tuberculosis Fever helps the body to fight infection Try to find and treat the cause of the fever

assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NEXT_TRANSPORT

---
Bulging fontanelle, stiff neck and vomiting point to meningitis. Send her on tomorrow's boat to hospital.
Malaria can cause this picture too, so give artemether-lumefantrine now if you have it, but do not delay the referral.
Keep breastfeeding small amounts if she can suck. Watch for convulsions, deeper drowsiness or stopping feeds.
Call the hospital radio tonight to warn them she is coming. Keep her cool but warm enough, and write times of all events.

[guideline: BREAST FEEDING p26] PROMOTE BREAST FEEDING - It is safe, simple, readily available and cheap - It contains all the nutrients that the baby needs to grow - It reduces the risk of diarrhoea, pneumonia, malnutrition and other diseases - Helps encourage bonding between mother and baby FACTS ABOUT BREAST FEEDING - Breast feeding should begin within the first hour after delivery - The first yellow milk a mother makes (colostrum) should be given to the baby. o It should not be thrown away as it contains important immunoglobulins that are part of the baby's defense against infection - The easiest and best schedule is 'on-demand' breast feeding o Infants who cannot demand feed (such as low birth weight or sick babies) should be fed every 2-3 hours o Infants who cannot suck on the breast (eg. very premature babies) should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup/spoon or by NG tube - Ideally all babies should be exclusively breast fed for the first 6 months o Solids should be introduced from 6 months o Cow's milk or powdered milk should be avoided before the age of 12 months because of the risk of iron-deficiency anaemia - Breast feeding should continue for as long as possible. - Breast feeding policies should be supported and upheld always - Bottles with teats and baby cups with spouts should discouraged. o They are difficult to sterilize and may result in infections such as diarrhoea - For facts about breast feeding in HIV positive mothers

I took a photo of the chest X-ray for a 10 month old boy with cough and fever. The family brought the film from the health centre. Can you look at the picture and tell me if it is pneumonia or TB, and what medicine to start?

ACTION: ASK_PERSON
STM: NONE
---
I am not sure, I cannot read X-ray pictures and no guideline came up for this.
Please send the film and the child's story to the doctor at the AHC or NRH by phone or radio, and tell them: boy 10 months, cough, fever, X-ray film from health centre.
The doctor will read the film and decide about pneumonia or TB treatment.
Meanwhile count his breathing, look for chest indrawing and check if he is feeding.
If he has chest indrawing, fast breathing or is not feeding, refer him now.

[guideline: BREAST FEEDING p26] DIFFICULTY BREAST FEEDING - Check the baby for underlying causes and treat: o Premature or low birth weight o Birth trauma o Infections (especially respiratory, meningitis, urinary tract infection) o Congenital problems such as cleft lip/ palate (feed with cup & spoon, refer to hospital) and trisomy 21 - Check the mother for any underlying problems (treat if possible, refer to midwife, paediatric nurse, paediatrician or obstetrician) o Maternal illness o Breast problem (cracked, flat or inverted nipples) o Adopting mother, never previously lactated - Problems with 'inadequate' milk supply o Check baby is sucking frequently and well (check positioning/ attachment) o Check to see if breast milk supply is really inadequate. If poor milk supply: - Consider giving the mother a trial of metoclopramide 10 mg tds OR chlorpromazine 25mg tds (until the breast milk supply increases) - Encourage mother to suckle the baby frequently, even if there is no breast milk to begin with o Baby formula should only be used if prescribed by a doctor
Six month old, 5.1 kg, mother worried her milk is drying up. Baby was gaining before but now stopped. I checked positioning, attachment looks poor. We have RDT and ACT here. Hospital boat can take them in one hour.
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: BREAST FEEDING
---
Fix the attachment first: baby's mouth should cover most of the areola, chin touching breast, nose free. Metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily for mother to build supply. She must feed very often day and night, even if she thinks milk is little. No formula without doctor. Return in 2 days to check weight; go to hospital now if baby refuses feeds, has fits, or cannot wake properly.

SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Fever, cough,fast breathing, increased work of breathing - Poor feeding, vomiting, chest or abdominal pain SEVERITY OF PNEUMONIA MILD MODERATE SEVERE Respiratory rate Normal or increased Increased Markedly increased Accessory muscle use Mild or absent Mild-moderate Markedly increased - intercostal recession - subcostal recession - nasal flare - grunting, head bob Oral intake Normal or reduced Often reduced Reduced/no intake Cyanosis Not present Unlikely May be present Conscious state Alert, active Usually alert Drowsy/lethargic May be distressed/agitated
Boy 48 months, about 14.5 kg. Cough for four days and skin hot since yesterday. He is drinking and still playing a bit, no fit, no vomiting everything. Breathing looks a little fast to me. What should I check and give?
assistant:
ACTION: ADVISE
STM: PNEUMONIA
---
Count his breathing for one full minute and look for recession, nasal flare and grunting, and check if he is drowsy.
If feeding is normal, no cyanosis and he is alert, this fits mild pneumonia.
Give amoxycillin 580 mg (40 mg/kg) by mouth every 12 hours for 7 days.
Give paracetamol 15 mg/kg every 6 hours if the skin is hot.
Come back in 2 days, or sooner if he stops drinking, vomits everything, breathes fast at rest, or becomes sleepy.

[guideline: PERTUSSIS (WHOOPING COUGH) p81] Whooping cough occurs when the bacteria Bordetella pertussis gets into the respiratory tract and causes a bloody mucous to be formed CAUSE - Spread by air droplets - Patients are contagious for 21 days after the onset of the cough, if untreated - Non-vaccinated children most commonly affected. Can occur in immunised children but usually a more mild illness SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Cough and runny nose for 1 week (1st stage) followed by spasmodic cough with 'whooping' sound. May also present as a non-specific persistant cough - Vomiting often following a coughing spasm - Apnoea or cyanosis during coughing spasms - Fever is uncommon - There may be no clinical signs on examination and children may appear well between coughing spasms COMPLICATIONS - Infants < 6 months are at greatest risk and are commonly infected by family members - Apnoea - Severe pneumonia - Encephalopathy INVESTIGATIONS - Generally a clinical diagnosis - If persistant cough or other suggestive symptoms (weight loss, night sweats) remember to assess TB exposure and consider investigations if risk factors - Blood count (may be associated with high lymphocyte count) MANAGEMENT MANAGEMENT NOTES:

[guideline: MENINGITIS p62] Meningitis is a very severe infection of the coverings of the brain (meninges) CAUSES - Bacteria (e.g: Meningoccous, Pneumococcus, Haemophilus, E.Coli) - Malaria (meningitis can be a complication cerebral malaria) - Viruses (e.g: enterovirus, HSV, VZ) - Tuberculosis - Fungus (e.g. cryptococcus) SIGNS & SYMPTOMS - Fever, headache, irritability, lethergy - Poor feeding, vomiting or diarrhoea - Bulging fontanelle (infants) - Photophobia, neck stiffness (older children) - Convulsions, decreased concious state
6 year old boy, 21 kg. He came with fever, severe headache, and his neck is very stiff. He vomited everything just now and looks drowsy. The truck is here now. What do I give before he goes?
assistant:
ACTION: REFER_NOW
STM: MENINGITIS
---
Stiff neck, vomiting everything and drowsiness are danger signs. Put him in the truck to hospital immediately.
Give ceftriaxone 2 g IV if you have it, or ampicillin 1 g IV now before he leaves. Give nothing by mouth because he vomits everything.
Place him on his side in case he vomits again during the trip. Keep him warm and keep the truck windows down for air.
Write the referral note: age 6 years, 21 kg, stiff neck, photophobia if present, drowsy, drug and time given. Call ahead to the hospital.

[guideline: NEWBORN BABIES LESS THAN 2.5 KG WEIGHT p66] Babies with low birth weight need special care. They are at risk of becoming cold (hypothermia), having low blood sugar (hypoglycaemia) and infection. Some babies are small because they are born prematurely (before they are due). Infection is an important cause of premature labour. MANAGEMENT - Keep the baby warm - Small babies get cold easily. o Keep the baby skin to skin when possible (together with mother or father) well wrapped up in a warm room. - Start feeds within 1 hour of delivery o Babies who can suck should be breastfed. o Babies who cannot be breastfed should be given expressed breast milk (EBM) by cup and spoon. Change to breastfeeding when the baby starts to suck well from the breast. o Use a NG tube for those less than 1.5kg, or not taking EBM well by cup and spoon or are sick. Nasogastric tubes should be changed twice a week. When the baby can suck well, change to breast feeding or cup and spoon o If EBM unavailable consider IV access and fluids, transfer to hospital

Sapos hem fit fo dring, givim EBM long cup an spun.
Sapos hem no dring, no forcim. Lukluk brit an warmth.

[guideline: CONVULSIONS p34] MANAGEMENT Make sure child is breathing; If not, give breaths using bag and mask Give oxygen IV 0.2mg/kg (max 10mg) OR PR 0.3mg/kg (max 10mg) Never give diazepam IM Drugs given rectally are best given using a syringe with feeding tube cut at a short length (insert 4-5cm into rectum) If still fitting after 10 minutes Give a second dose of midazolam/diazepam Do not give more than 2 doses of diazepam If still fitting after 20 minutes IM/IV phenobarbitone (loading 20mg/kg over 15 mins, max 1g) OR IV phenytoin (loading dose 20mg/kg over 60 mins) Ensure a good IV line as phenytoin is damaging if IV leaks into skin Ensure also it is given in a different line to diazapam Once fitting stops Check temperature. If fever, look for a cause of the fever Consider investigation and treatment for malaria Consider a lumbar puncture and treatment for meningitis Consider epilepsy in the child who has had previous seizures without fever
